passages.happening:
Jesus says, “I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard” (verse 1).

The Father deals with the branches in two ways. Every branch in Jesus that bears no fruit, he cuts off. Every branch that does bear fruit, he prunes, “to make it even more fruitful” (verse 2).

“You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you” (verse 3). Then comes the heart of it: “Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Everyone in the room knew vines. They grew on terraced hillsides all over Judea and Galilee. Every farmer knew that a vine has to be cut back hard, or it runs to leaves and wood and gives few grapes. And everyone knew that a branch broken off the vine is dead, however green it looks for a day or two.

The vine was also a picture of Israel itself. Over the doorway into the holy place of Herod's temple hung a great golden vine. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the first century, describes it, with golden clusters of grapes he says were as tall as a man. When Jesus says ‘I am the true vine’, his hearers would think of that vine, and of their people.

‘True’ in John does not mean that what came before was false. It means the real thing that earlier things pointed to. Jesus calls himself ‘the true bread’ in the same way (6:32), and that does not make the manna in the desert false. Jesus does not say Israel is a false vine. He says that he is the vine in whom Israel's calling comes true. He and every person listening to him are Jews.

‘Clean’ (verse 3) and ‘prunes’ (verse 2) are close in Greek: kathairei, ‘he prunes’, and katharoi, ‘clean’. Jesus is playing on the words. The disciples have already been pruned, made clean, by his word.

‘Remain’ is John's great word, often translated ‘abide’. It means to stay, to live in, to make your home. Jesus uses it ten times in the first ten verses of this chapter in the Greek.
passages.ot:
The prophets often called Israel God's vine. A psalm prays, “You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it” (Psalm 80:8). Then it grieves, “Your vine has been cut down and burned” (Psalm 80:16), and asks God to help “the son of man You have raised up for Yourself” (Psalm 80:17).

Isaiah sang a love song about God's vineyard. God did everything for it, “He waited for the vineyard to yield good grapes, but the fruit it produced was sour” (Isaiah 5:2). “For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7). Jeremiah grieved, “How could you turn yourself before Me into a rotten, wild vine?” (Jeremiah 2:21). And Isaiah also promised a day when God would sing over a fruitful vineyard: “I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually” (Isaiah 27:3).

Where Israel's story had sour grapes, Jesus says: I am the vine that bears the fruit God was looking for, and you can bear it too, in me.
passages.hard:
Does the Father ‘cut off’ or ‘lift up’ the fruitless branch? The Greek verb in verse 2, airei, can mean ‘take away’ or ‘lift up’. The Berean Standard Bible says ‘cuts off’, as most English Bibles do.

Some readers prefer ‘lifts up’. They note that this is the word's first meaning, and that vine growers lift trailing branches off the ground so that they get light and air and begin to bear. On this reading the Father first lifts and cares for the branch that has no fruit.

Most translators and many scholars read ‘takes away’. They note that the word often means that, and that verse 6 speaks of branches thrown away and burned, which suggests removal in verse 2 too.

Both readings are held by careful Christians. These notes take no side. Either way, the Father is the gardener, and his work on the fruitful branches is pruning: painful, and for their good.
passages.asks: Pruning hurts, and it is done by a gardener who wants fruit, not by an enemy. Ask whether something in your life is being cut back, and whether you can trust the gardener with it. And notice the simplest command in the chapter: remain. Not ‘produce’, but stay. The fruit comes from the vine.

passages.t: Apart from Me you can do nothing
passages.happening:
“I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing” (verse 5).

Then a warning: “If anyone does not remain in Me, he is like a branch that is thrown away and withers. Such branches are gathered up, thrown into the fire, and burned” (verse 6).

And a promise: “If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you” (verse 7). The Father is glorified when they bear much fruit and so show that they are Jesus' disciples (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Vine wood is good for nothing but the fire. You cannot build with it or carve it. A branch cut off a vine is not used for anything else. It is gathered and burned. Every hearer knew that.

What is the ‘fruit’? Jesus does not list it here, but the chapter points to it: love for one another (verses 12 and 17), answered prayer that glorifies the Father (verses 7-8), and joy (verse 11). Later Paul names ‘the fruit of the Spirit’: love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Galatians 5:22-23). Fruit is not the same as busy activity or success. It is the life of Jesus showing in a person.

The promise ‘ask whatever you wish’ comes with its condition: ‘If you remain in Me and My words remain in you’. A person whose life is shaped by Jesus' words learns to want what he wants. The notes on 14:13-14, Mark 11 and Matthew 7 explain that this is not a promise that God will give anything we demand.
passages.ot: Ezekiel asks, “how does the wood of the vine surpass any other branch among the trees in the forest?” His answer: “No, it is cast into the fire for fuel” (Ezekiel 15:2, 15:4). Without fruit, a vine branch has no other use.
passages.hard:
Can a true believer ever be lost? Verse 6 is one of the passages Christians turn to when they ask this, and they have answered differently for centuries. Each answer is held by faithful churches. The views are given here as their own teachers state them.

Many Reformed and Calvinist churches teach the perseverance of the saints. The Westminster Confession, chapter 17, says that those God has truly called and made holy ‘can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace’. They read the branches that are thrown away as people joined to Jesus only outwardly, like Judas, who had just gone out into the night (13:30). They point to 10:28 and to 1 John 2:19: “They went out from us, but they did not belong to us.”

Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Wesleyan and Methodist churches, and many others, teach that a believer can fall away. They read the branches as real branches, truly joined to the vine, who stop remaining in him. They hear verse 6 as a real warning, given in love.

Some others read the fire as a picture of a believer's wasted life and lost reward, not of final judgment.

All sides agree on what the passage most plainly says. Life comes only from remaining in Jesus, and the warning is given to draw his friends closer, not to drive them away. These notes do not settle the question between them. It is a question faithful Christians have long differed on, open for discussion and not a cause for division.

If this verse frightens you, notice who Jesus is speaking to: friends he loves (verse 9), already clean (verse 3). The warning is not meant to make you anxious about whether you are good enough. It is meant to send you to him. Anyone who is afraid of being cut off can do the one thing the chapter asks: come back to the vine, and stay.
passages.asks: ‘Apart from Me you can do nothing.’ Ask where you are trying to bear fruit on your own: being patient, being kind, keeping going, by willpower alone. The branch does not strain to produce grapes. It stays joined to the vine. Ask what it would look like this week to stay close to Jesus: in his words, in prayer, among his people.

passages.happening:
“As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love” (verse 9). They remain in his love by keeping his commandments, as he has kept his Father's. He tells them this “so that My joy may be in you and your joy may be complete” (verse 11).

His commandment is this: love one another as he has loved them (verse 12). “Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (verse 13). “You are My friends if you do what I command you” (verse 14).

“No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you” (verse 15).

“You did not choose Me, but I chose you” (verse 16). He appointed them to go and bear fruit that will last. “This is My command to you: Love one another” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
In that world a servant, or slave, did what he was told without being told why. A friend was let into the master's plans. Kings in the Greek world even had an inner circle of trusted advisers who were officially called ‘Friends’, and the title ‘friend of Caesar’ (19:12) comes from the same world. Jesus is saying: I have let you into everything. You are in the inner circle.

‘Greater love has no one than this’ would have sounded to many in that world like the highest ideal of friendship: to die for a friend. Jesus says it hours before he does it. And Paul adds something stranger: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). He laid down his life for friends who were about to run away.

‘You did not choose Me, but I chose you’ may have sounded unusual too. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, advises a student to find himself a teacher, which suggests that students usually sought out their teachers. Jesus did it the other way round. He went and found his disciples, and called them (1:43).

‘You are My friends if you do what I command you’ is not a test to earn friendship. He has already called them friends. It describes what friends of Jesus look like: people who do what he asks, and what he asks is love.
passages.ot: Only a few people in the Old Testament are called God's friends. God calls Abraham “Abraham My friend” (Isaiah 41:8), and “the LORD would speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Exodus 33:11). Jesus now gives that name to a group of ordinary men, fishermen among them.
passages.asks: Jesus calls you his friend, not his servant, and he gave his life to prove it. Ask whether you relate to him as a nervous servant, afraid of getting it wrong, or as a friend he has let into his plans. And ask whom you are laying down your life for, in small ways, today: your time, your comfort, your right to be first.

passages.happening:
“If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first” (verse 18). If they belonged to the world, the world would love them as its own. But Jesus has chosen them out of the world, so the world hates them (verse 19).

He reminds them of what he said at the foot washing: “No servant is greater than his master” (verse 20). If people persecuted him, they will persecute them. If people kept his word, they will keep theirs.

They will treat them like this because of his name, because they do not know the one who sent him (verse 21). If he had not come and spoken and done his works, they would not be guilty; now they have no excuse (verses 22-24). This fulfils what is written in their Law: “They hated Me without reason” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
‘The world’ in John does not mean the earth, or any one nation, or people who are not Christians. Often it means human life organized without God and against him. God loves that world so much that he gave his Son for it (3:16). So ‘the world hates you’ never gives Christians leave to hate anyone back, or to look down on outsiders, or to treat every disagreement as persecution. Jesus has just told his followers to love. The same Jesus told them to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44).

The first Christians did suffer for his name. The book of Acts tells of arrests and beatings by the temple authorities, the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7:58-60), and King Herod putting James the brother of John to death with the sword (Acts 12:2). Later, Roman rulers put Christians to death too. In many places Christians still suffer for their faith today.

‘Their Law’ here means the Scriptures as a whole, not only the five books of Moses. The words Jesus quotes come from the Psalms.
passages.ot: ‘They hated Me without reason’ is found in the Psalms. David says, “Those who hate me without cause outnumber the hairs of my head” (Psalm 69:4), and prays against “those who hate me without reason” (Psalm 35:19). The innocent sufferer of the Psalms, hated for no wrong he had done, is a picture of Jesus.
passages.hard:
Does this mean Christians should expect everyone to hate them? No. Jesus says ‘if’, and he says that some will keep their word (verse 20). Many people will listen. And not every hard time a Christian has is persecution. Sometimes people dislike Christians because Christians have behaved badly. The New Testament asks believers to live at peace with everyone as far as they can (Romans 12:18), and to answer with ‘gentleness and respect’ (1 Peter 3:15-16).

But some hatred is simply because of Jesus' name. For anyone who suffers that, at school, at work, in a family or under a government, Jesus' words are a comfort: you are not alone, and he went first.
passages.asks: If you are suffering because you belong to Jesus, he says: it hated me first. You are walking where he walked. And if you are tempted to see yourself as a victim every time someone disagrees with you, ask honestly whether the world is hating Jesus in you, or simply reacting to something in you that is not like him.

passages.happening:
“When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father”, Jesus says, he will be “the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father”, and “He will testify about Me” (verse 26).

“And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
In a world that hates him, Jesus does not leave his friends to defend him alone. The Spirit, the Advocate, will be a witness, and so will they. Remember that ‘advocate’ is a courtroom word, someone who stands beside you and speaks for you. John's book is full of trial language: witness, testify, judge. Here the trial goes on after Jesus leaves, and he provides the witnesses.

The disciples' witness matters because they were there ‘from the beginning’. This is why the church has always cared about eyewitnesses. John's book ends by saying, ‘This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down’ (21:24).

‘Who proceeds from the Father’ became important in a long debate between the churches of the East and the West. The Nicene Creed, in the older English wording printed on this site, confesses the Spirit as the one ‘who proceedeth from the Father’. Many Western churches add ‘and the Son’; the Eastern Orthodox churches do not. Both confess the Spirit as fully God, ‘worshipped and glorified’ with the Father and the Son.
passages.ot: The Law required more than one witness to settle a matter: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus gives two: the Spirit, and the disciples.
passages.asks: Witnesses do not make the truth; they tell what they have seen. Ask what you have seen of Jesus that you could tell someone, simply and honestly. And notice that you do not testify alone. The Spirit of truth goes before you.
